title: Data Science
text: Data Science — HSC Final Notes ✅ Named topic in the Trial (Task 4). 80 marks · 30% · 2½ hrs incl. 10 min reading · online , practical and theoretical. Outcomes: EC-12-02, EC-12-03, EC-12-04, EC-12-05, EC-12-07 Terminology: Terminology · Index: MOC 1. Ethical Issues in Data Use The ethical use of data means ensuring fairness, accuracy, and respect for privacy and ownership. 1.1 The Seven Ethical Principles Principle Definition Consent Participants are informed about the purpose of the research, the data collected and how it will be used, and give informed consent Confidentiality Researchers maintain the confidentiality of participants and their data unless otherwise agreed or required by law Privacy Collection, storage and use of personal data respects individuals' privacy and complies with data protection laws Data accuracy Data collected is accurate and reliable, minimising potential harm to participants Data security Collected data is stored securely and protected against unauthorised access, loss or theft Transparency Researchers are open about their methods, results and any potential biases Responsibility Researchers take responsibility for the consequences of their research Confusing pair — Confidentiality vs Privacy Privacy is the individual's right to control their personal information. Confidentiality is the researcher's obligation not to disclose it. Privacy belongs to the person. Confidentiality is a duty owed to them. 1.2 The Seven Ethical Issues Issue What it means Bias Systematic unfairness arising from how data is collected, processed or interpreted. Leads to discrimination. Addressed through diverse and representative datasets and awareness of prejudice in algorithms Accuracy of collected data Inaccurate data produces incorrect conclusions. Addressed through regular validation, cleaning and cross-referencing with reliable sources Metadata Data about other data — how, when and by whom it was collected. Proper management ensures transparency and improves data governance Copyright and acknowledgement of source data Citing sources accurately and adhering to licensing agreements to avoid legal issues and credit original providers Intellectual property and ICIP IP laws protect data creators. Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property recognises the right of Indigenous communities to control cultural heritage and traditional knowledge. Requires obtaining consent and acknowledging ownership Permissions, rights and privacy of individuals Including cultural responsibility — handling data in ways that respect cultural protocols Security Protecting data from unauthorised access, breaches and cyber attack Confusing term — Metadata : data that describes other data. A photo's metadata includes the date, camera model and GPS location. Metadata is an ethical issue because it can identify people even when the underlying data is anonymised. 1.3 Software Features Affecting Privacy and Security Feature Risks Mitigation Autofill Data leakage if a device is lost or stolen · exploited by phishing to capture credentials on fake sites · unwanted sharing on shared or public devices · saves a record of everything entered Disable on public and shared browsers, review and delete saved data, use a password manager with encryption and two-factor authentication Public or private connections Public Wi-Fi (airports, cafés, hotels) is generally unsecured — data can be intercepted. Private networks are more secure but can still be hacked or infected with malware Encryption via a VPN before transmission · firewalls to block unauthorised access · awareness of the risks of each connection type Checkbox Users may inadvertently consent to data collection or third-party sharing without understanding the implications Read before ticking; understand what each box authorises Terms of agreement (TOA) Specify what data is collected , how it is shared with partners, affiliates and advertisers, and retention and deletion policies. Users who don't read them may unknowingly consent Read and understand before accepting. In some cases users can negotiate terms or seek alternative agreements 2. Legal Issues in Data Use 2.1 Legislation Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) — the primary Australian law governing how personal information is collected, used, stored and disclosed. Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) — 13 principles governing: 1. The collection, use and disclosure of personal information 2. An organisation or agency's governance and accountability 3. Integrity and correction of personal information 4. The rights of individuals to access their personal information Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) scheme — requires entities to notify affected individuals and the OAIC about data breaches likely to result in serious harm . 2.2 Authorities Responsible for Data Protection Authority Role Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) The key authority. Enforces the Privacy Act , investigates complaints, and issues guidelines and resources for compliance 2.3 Data Sovereignty of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples Indigenous data sovereignty is the right of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to control the collection, ownership and application of data about their communities. Consideration Requirement Informed consent Data collection conducted with the community's informed consent, not just an individual's Cultural respect Data handled in ways that respect cultural protocols and values Control and ownership Communities empowered to manage and decide how their data is used and accessed Confusing pair — ICIP vs Data sovereignty ICIP protects Indigenous cultural knowledge and heritage as intellectual property. Data sovereignty is the broader right to control data about the community itself — who collects it, who owns it, how it's used. ICIP is about the content. Sovereignty is about the control. 3. Social Issues — Curated and Communicated Data 3.1 The Core Distinction Definition Effect Curated data Data that has been selected , with context removed and the message simplified for impact Persuasive. Creates strong signals, encourages conformity Communicated data Data presented with context and explanation — sample size, timeframe, limitations Informative. Meaning is clearer and less misleading Curated data is not fake — it is selective. That distinction is examinable. Worked example. A post reads: "80% of students say AI tools make learning easier." CURATED (what was shared) "80% of students say AI tools make learning easier" COMMUNICATED (what was hidden) Sample size: 50 students Year conducted: 2 years ago Limitations of the poll The curated version moves data from informative to persuasive . 3.2 The Five Social Factors Factor What it does Data literacy Determines whether data informs or influences . Data-literate users question the source, notice missing context and recognise signal manipulation. Less literate users accept the signal at face value and change behaviour without questioning Timeframes When data is shared changes how people react. Shared too late, people can't act. Outdated data exaggerates relevance, misguides decisions and creates false confidence Signals impacting behaviour A figure like "80%" acts as a social signal suggesting what is normal, popular or acceptable. Signals influence behaviour even when data quality is weak Data swamps Too much unorganised, undocumented or irrelevant data, making useful information hard to find. Systems trained on a data swamp repeat outdated assumptions, amplify weak signals and make poor recommendations Educating users Teaching people how data works and how to interpret it helps them make smarter choices and protect their privacy Confusing pair — Data warehouse vs Data swamp A data warehouse is a structured, documented central repository built for analysis. A data swamp is an unmanaged accumulation — no documentation, no clarity of purpose. Same volume, opposite governance. 4. Data Types and Levels of Measurement 4.1 Quantitative vs Qualitative Definition Examples Quantitative Numerical — can be counted or measured Scores, counts, dates, prices, temperatures Qualitative Descriptive — categories, text, observations Comments, feedback, colours, categories, opinions 4.2 The Four Levels of Measurement Level Definition Can you… Example Nominal Named categories with no order Count only Eye colour, house, gender, suburb Ordinal Categories with a meaningful order , but unequal gaps Rank Satisfaction (poor/fair/good), year level, medal placing Interval Ordered, equal gaps , but no true zero Add and subtract Temperature in °C, calendar years, IQ Ratio Ordered, equal gaps, true zero Add, subtract, multiply, divide Height, weight, price, age, count The test for interval vs ratio: does zero mean "none of it"? 0 kg means no mass → ratio . 0 °C does not mean no temperature → interval . You cannot say "20 °C is twice as hot as 10 °C", but you can say "20 kg is twice 10 kg". 4.3 Structured, Unstructured and Alternative Data Type Definition Examples Structured Organised in a fixed format — rows, columns, fields Databases, spreadsheets, tables Unstructured No fixed format, variable length Text, comments, images, video, memes Alternative Non-traditional feedback signals from a different format or source Likes, emoticons, memes , click counts, sentiment labels Alternative data as feedback: Likes — indicate approval or support. The count gauges popularity and public response Emoticons — pictorial representations of emotion. Provide insight into users' emotional responses , opinions and attitudes Memes — images, video or text spread virally, often satirical. Popularity measures public interest and reveals opinion and attitudes 4.4 Informatics Informatics is the study of the processing and management of information . It provides tools and techniques supporting the collection, organisation, analysis and interpretation of data. Why it matters: without informatics, different data types remain disconnected and meaningless . Informatics enables a system to integrate, analyse and interpret diverse sources to produce informed outcomes. On structured data On unstructured data Organise into entities, attributes and keys Categorise or tag data Apply queries — filtering, sorting, aggregation Convert into semi-structured or structured form Support rule-based decisions (IF–THEN) Link user feedback to system rules or outcomes Example: visitor counts, timestamps and locations analysed to identify peak times and trigger automated decisions Example: likes, emojis and comments interpreted as positive, neutral or negative and stored as sentiment values the system can reason with 5. Databases and SQL 5.1 Flat-file vs Relational Flat-file Relational (RDBMS) Structure A single table or file — plain text, CSV, JSON Multiple linked tables Relationships None Tables linked by keys Duplication High Reduced Indexing None Yes Best for Small, simple datasets, prototypes Enterprise-scale data, accuracy and organisation 5.2 Keys Key Rules Purpose Primary key Uniquely identifies each row · cannot be NULL · cannot be duplicated Ensures each record is unique; maintains data integrity Foreign key Refers to a primary key in another table Links related data ; creates the relationship between tables Composite key Two or more fields together forming the primary key Used in join tables resolving many-to-many relationships Example: Results.StudentID (foreign key) → Students.StudentID (primary key). 5.3 Relationships and Normalisation Relationship Handling One to many (1:∞) The most common. Each record in the primary key's table can have many matching records in the foreign key's table One to one (1:1) Always possible — and usually preferable — to combine both tables into one Many to many (∞:∞) Cannot be implemented directly. Must be resolved by creating a join table with two 1:∞ relationships, containing foreign keys to both original primary keys. Together these form a composite primary key Normalisation improves a database's efficiency, consistency and accuracy, and makes it adaptable to changing enterprise needs. Why redundancy is a problem: repeated data unnecessarily increases database size, and causes inconsistency during insert, delete and update operations . Worked normalisation: Problem Solution Identical rows — can't tell orders apart Add an OrderID to uniquely identify each order An Order column contains multiple values (non-atomic) Move the order items to a separate table Customer Name is a composite value Break into First Name and Last Name columns Repeated values for the same customer Move customer details to their own table, link by key Data dictionary — documents the structure of the database: field names, data types, data format and other attributes. Serves as a reference ensuring consistency and shared understanding of the design. 5.4 SQL — LibreOffice Base ⚠️ Mixed-case names and names with spaces must be in double quotes: "YearLevel" , "Student Name" . Text values use single quotes: 'Blue' . Basic SELECT SELECT * FROM "Students"; SELECT "FirstName", "LastName", "YearLevel" FROM "Students"; WHERE — filtering SELECT * FROM "Students" WHERE "YearLevel" = 12; SELECT "FirstName", "LastName" FROM "Students" WHERE "YearLevel" = 12 AND "House" = 'Blue'; WHERE "LastName" LIKE 'Sm%'; -- text matching, % is the wildcard ORDER BY, DISTINCT, LIMIT SELECT "StudentID", "Score" FROM "Results" ORDER BY "Score" DESC; SELECT DISTINCT "House" FROM "Students"; ORDER BY "Score" DESC LIMIT 5; -- may not work on all drivers SELECT "StudentID", "Score" FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY; -- fallback Aggregates and GROUP BY SELECT "Task", AVG("Score") AS "AvgScore" FROM "Results" GROUP BY "Task"; SELECT "YearLevel", COUNT(*) AS "NumStudents" FROM "Students" GROUP BY "YearLevel"; HAVING — filtering groups SELECT "Task", AVG("Score") AS "AvgScore" FROM "Results" GROUP BY "Task" HAVING AVG("Score") >= 70; Confusing pair — WHERE vs HAVING WHERE filters individual rows , before grouping. HAVING filters groups , after GROUP BY has aggregated them. You cannot use an aggregate function in WHERE . JOINs -- INNER JOIN: only rows with matches in BOTH tables SELECT s."FirstName", s."LastName", r."Task", r."Score" FROM "Students" s INNER JOIN "Results" r ON s."StudentID" = r."StudentID"; -- LEFT JOIN: ALL students, even those with no results SELECT s."FirstName", s."LastName", r."Task", r."Score" FROM "Students" s LEFT JOIN "Results" r ON s."StudentID" = r."StudentID"; JOIN + WHERE + ORDER BY — the common report query SELECT s."FirstName", s."LastName", r."Task", r."Score" FROM "Students" s INNER JOIN "Results" r ON s."StudentID" = r."StudentID" WHERE s."YearLevel" = 12 ORDER BY r."Score" DESC; JOIN + GROUP BY — averages per student SELECT s."StudentID", s."FirstName", s."LastName", AVG(r."Score") AS "AvgScore" FROM "Students" s INNER JOIN "Results" r ON s."StudentID" = r."StudentID" GROUP BY s."StudentID", s."FirstName", s."LastName"; Three-table JOIN SELECT s."FirstName", s."LastName", c."ClassName", r."Task", r."Score" FROM "Students" s INNER JOIN "Classes" c ON s."ClassID" = c."ClassID" INNER JOIN "Results" r ON s."StudentID" = r."StudentID" ORDER BY c."ClassName", s."LastName"; INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE INSERT INTO "MOVIE" ("MovieID", "Title", "Genre", "Rating") VALUES (1, 'Inception', 'Sci-Fi', 'M'); UPDATE "MOVIE" SET "Rating" = 'MA15+' WHERE "MovieID" = 1; DELETE FROM "MOVIE" WHERE "MovieID" = 1; LibreOffice Base gotchas: query errors are usually quotes — use "FieldName" for mixed case or spaces. "Table not found" means the exact name doesn't match the Tables list. LIMIT may fail on some drivers, so use FETCH FIRST . 6. Spreadsheets and Dashboards 6.1 The Key Rule One sheet = one table = one purpose. Even though spreadsheets are flat-file systems, multiple sheets let you separate data types, reduce repetition, improve clarity and support decision logic. Data type How to store it Structured — numeric or categorical, consistent format Directly in tables Unstructured — text-based, descriptive, variable length As text fields, not mixed with numbers Alternative — click counts, frequency totals, sentiment labels Often generated or summarised from other data 6.2 Linking Sheets Without SQL Spreadsheets use logical links , not joins: Matching IDs (e.g. RecordID) VLOOKUP / XLOOKUP FILTER COUNTIF, AVERAGEIF 6.3 Summary Statistics Function Returns SUM Total of values COUNT Number of data points AVERAGE The mean — typical value MIN / MAX The range 6.4 Analysis Features Feature Use Charts Transform numerical data into visual form so patterns, comparisons and trends are easier to see Pivot tables Interactive summarising of large datasets without formulas . Drag-and-drop fields to build instant, filterable reports (e.g. total sales by region) Slicers Interactive filter buttons for a pivot table or dashboard Conditional formatting Automatically highlight cells meeting a condition What-if modelling Change inputs to see the effect on outputs — scenario testing Forms and reports Present data clearly for entry and for output Chart selection: Chart Shows Scatter chart Relationships, trends and patterns between variables Histogram Data distribution — detects skewness and outliers Line graph Change over time Filtering displays only specific parts of a dataset. It can lead to biased conclusions if too much data is excluded — that limitation is examinable. 7. Data Scale and Big Data 7.1 The Impact of Data Scale Aspect The issue Volume of raw data More records improve accuracy, but extreme size degrades system performance and increases cost Storage Insufficient storage limits decision-making; storage choice affects speed and scalability; loss or corruption is catastrophic Real-time and continuous streaming Delayed data can be useless. Data that never stops arriving creates technical challenges and drives system design Opportunities for machine learning ML requires large datasets . Poor-quality data produces poor predictions Changes in human behaviour Behaviour change increases volume and velocity, and modern data is increasingly unstructured Ethical implications, incl. digital footprints Scale increases privacy risk and makes bias harder to detect 7.2 Big Data — The Three Vs VOLUME the amount of data VARIETY the range of types and sources VELOCITY the speed at which it arrives and must be processed Data warehouse — a central repository storing large volumes of historical and current data from multiple sources. Advantages Limitations Supports complex queries · enables trend analysis · improves decision accuracy Complex to implement · requires skilled design · higher cost 8. Data Sampling and Storage 8.1 Sampling Data sampling is selecting a subset of data from a larger dataset so decisions can be made efficiently without analysing everything. Active collection Passive collection Definition Collected intentionally from users Collected automatically , without direct user input Examples Surveys, forms, questionnaires, user input fields System logs, sensor data, clickstream data, usage analytics Strengths More control Large volume, real-time Weaknesses Can introduce bias ; depends on user participation Privacy concerns ; less user awareness Method Description Limitation Manual A human selects and records data Time-consuming, error-prone Computerised Software collects and samples automatically Bias if poorly designed Poor sampling produces incorrect recommendations, biased outcomes and unreliable system behaviour. Effective sampling ensures decisions are representative, processing is efficient and the system scales. 8.2 Storage Methods Method Advantages Limitations Local storage Fast access · full control · no internet required Limited scalability · risk of data loss · unsuitable for large datasets or collaboration Cloud storage Scalable · accessible anywhere · supports collaboration and backups Internet dependency · ongoing cost · privacy and compliance concerns Portable storage media Portable · offline access · simple High risk of loss or theft · limited capacity · unsuitable for real-time systems Data warehouses Supports complex queries · enables trend analysis · improves decision accuracy Complex · requires skilled design · higher cost The judgements to make: local storage suits small-scale prototypes but limits scalability. Portable storage is generally unsuitable for a decision support system due to security and scalability risk. Cloud supports enterprise-scale systems. Data warehouses enable high-quality, enterprise-level decision support. 9. Errors, Uncertainty and Data Quality 9.1 The Three Problems Definition Errors Mistakes made in data collection, entry or processing — from minor typos to significant inaccuracies Uncertainty Lack of precision or ambiguity , arising from the measurement process, the nature of the data, or the analysis method Limitations Inherent constraints — sample size, coverage, representativeness, or the scope and reliability of the sources 9.2 Causes Cause Effect Data collection methods Self-reported data is subject to bias; observed data is subject to observer error Sample size Small samples may not represent the population, producing high uncertainty Data quality Poor accuracy or completeness produces errors and limitations Data timeliness Outdated data doesn't reflect current trends, impacting validity 9.3 Raw vs Processed Data Definition Risk Raw data Not processed or analysed in any way More susceptible to collection and entry errors; often not in an analysable format Processed data Cleaned, transformed or manipulated for analysis Processing reduces errors — but can introduce new uncertainty if methods are inappropriate or the data is manipulated unrepresentatively Data bias — systematic errors arising from selective sampling, underrepresentation of groups, or measurement error. Affects the validity of conclusions and may perpetuate or amplify existing inequalities . 9.4 The Four Quality Criteria Criterion The question Relevance Is the data relevant to the purpose? Accuracy Is it correct and error-free? Validity Does it measure what it's supposed to ? Reliability Would you get the same results collecting it again? 9.5 Primary vs Secondary Data Primary Secondary Definition Collected directly by you for a specific purpose Collected by someone else , used by you Examples Surveys, experiments, observations, interviews Books, journal articles, reports, government statistics Relevance Designed to address your question directly — highly relevant May not match your question, but gives useful background Accuracy Depends on careful collection; poor design produces poor data Harder to assess — you must trust the source Validity Ensured by designing collection to measure what you want May not be valid, as it wasn't collected with your question in mind Reliability Reliable if the method is well-structured and repeatable Reliable from credible sources using standardised, repeatable methods (e.g. ABS ) 9.6 The Data Quality Chain Data Collection (from different sources) ↓ Raw Data (unfiltered, uncleaned, incomplete) ↓ Data Processing (cleaning, sorting, filtering, summarising) ↓ Possible issues: errors · uncertainty · limitations · data bias ↓ Impact on quality: relevance · accuracy · validity · reliability ↓ Risk to decisions (incorrect or biased outputs) ↓ Need for data trust and verification → BLOCKCHAIN 10. Blockchain Blockchain is a distributed ledger that manages and verifies data in a secure, transparent and decentralised manner. Instead of a central server, it works peer-to-peer , with nodes communicating directly across the network. How it works: Transactions are verified and recorded as blocks Blocks are linked to form a chain Each block contains the hash of the previous block , so a previous block cannot be modified without invalidating every subsequent block Blocks are stored across multiple nodes , creating a decentralised ledger Transactions are confirmed by multiple participants , making falsification difficult Four Applications Application How blockchain is used Online voting Creates a secure, transparent record of voting transactions, making voting tamper-proof Online identities Digital identities stored as assets on the chain, authenticating individuals, organisations and devices. Offers greater security, privacy and control than traditional online identities Tracking items of value Assets represented by unique identifiers called tokens , verifying ownership and tracking transfers. Uses public ledgers and smart contracts Recordkeeping Maintaining and storing information in a secure, decentralised and tamper-proof manner 11. Data Mining, Machine Learning and Statistical Modelling Definition Data mining Discovering patterns, relationships and anomalies in large datasets Machine learning Uses algorithms to identify patterns and relationships in large datasets, improving with more data Statistical modelling Uses mathematical and statistical techniques to build models that make predictions Used together to analyse and predict from large datasets — customer behaviour, market trends, sales data. The resulting models help organisations identify trends and make data-driven decisions. Always state the limitation. Consider the biases that may exist in the data and the potential for errors in predictions . A model is only as good as the data behind it. 12. Confusing Terms — Quick Reference Term Meaning Don't confuse with Curated data Selected, context removed Communicated data — context included Data warehouse Structured, documented repository Data swamp — unmanaged accumulation Privacy The individual's right Confidentiality — the researcher's duty ICIP Indigenous cultural knowledge as IP Data sovereignty — the right to control the data itself Primary key Unique, not null, in this table Foreign key — refers to another table's primary key WHERE Filters rows, before grouping HAVING — filters groups, after INNER JOIN Only matching rows in both tables LEFT JOIN — all rows from the left table Interval Equal gaps, no true zero Ratio — has a true zero Nominal Categories, no order Ordinal — categories with order Active collection User intentionally supplies it Passive — collected automatically Raw data Unprocessed Processed — cleaned and transformed Errors Mistakes Uncertainty — imprecision · Limitations — inherent constraints Validity Measures what it should Reliability — repeatable results Flat-file One table, no relationships Relational — multiple linked tables Structured data Fixed format Unstructured — no format · Alternative — different source See also: Terminology | Intelligent Systems | Data Visualisation | Enterprise Project | MOC

title: Data Visualisation
text: Data Visualisation — HSC Final Notes ✅ Named topic in the Trial (Task 4). Six weeks. HSC 2025 exam: 14 marks across 6 questions. Key verbs: Describe, Explain . Online exam tools to be familiar with: screen design tool · drawing tool · spreadsheet tool Terminology: Terminology · Index: MOC 1. The Purposes of Data Visualisation Data visualisations transform raw data into a visual format, enabling users to quickly and effectively understand complex information. Presenting data graphically provides clarity and insight that would be difficult to discern in text or numerical form. The three purposes — memorise these Purpose How it is achieved Simplifying understanding Uses visual cues (colour, shape, size) so viewers identify patterns immediately without reading numbers · condenses large information into a compact format, reducing cognitive load · shows relationships by placing data points visually side by side · provides context by showing how individual points relate to the whole · makes data accessible to non-technical audiences Telling a story Contextualises data rather than presenting isolated numbers · shows change over time and comparison between groups · highlights trends and patterns · shows relationships between variables · uses colour, layout and design to make data engaging and memorable · communicates not just what the data shows but what it means and what action follows Highlighting significant results Emphasises key trends through line graphs · enables easy comparison through bar graphs where height indicates significance · makes outliers stand out · reveals patterns and correlations through heat maps and scatter plots · uses contrasting colour to distinguish high and low values 1.1 The Four-Step Answer Structure Every "explain how this visualisation…" question uses the same shape: 1. WHAT The visual shows… [identify the key feature] 2. HOW This is shown by… which indicates… [identify relationships] 3. WHY This means that… because… [cause and effect] 4. SO WHAT Therefore, the visualisation… [link to the purpose] Model answer — simplifying understanding This visual simplifies understanding by transforming complex data into an easy-to-read format using visual cues such as colours, shapes and sizes. The use of different colours and icons helps distinguish between categories, allowing viewers to quickly identify key information. Additionally, the visual condenses a large amount of data into a compact form, which reduces the need to interpret raw numbers. It also highlights relationships between data points by presenting them side by side, making comparisons and patterns easier to recognise. Therefore, the visual makes the data more accessible and allows users to quickly understand important information and trends. Model answer — telling a story (Minard's Napoleon map) This visual tells a story by showing Napoleon's army travelling to and from Russia while gradually decreasing in size. This is shown by the line becoming thinner as the journey progresses, indicating significant troop losses. The temperature graph also shows that as temperatures dropped, the size of the army decreased, highlighting a relationship between harsh weather conditions and losses. Additionally, the map provides context by showing the direction and location of the journey. Therefore, the visual effectively tells the story of the failed campaign by combining trends, relationships and contextual information to communicate the impact of the environment on the army. Model answer — highlighting significant results This visualisation highlights significant results by clearly comparing the popularity of different pizza toppings. This is shown through the use of a bar graph, where taller bars represent more popular toppings and shorter bars represent less popular ones. This makes it easy to identify key results, such as which toppings are most and least preferred. Additionally, some toppings stand out as outliers because they are significantly more or less popular than others, which helps to emphasise strong preferences. The visual also allows comparison between categories, such as meat and vegetable toppings, revealing patterns in consumer choices. Therefore, the visualisation effectively highlights significant results by using comparisons, visual features and patterns to draw attention to the most important insights in the data. Two classic examples to name: Playfair's trade balance chart (shading shows the crossover from deficit to surplus) and Minard's Napoleon map (line thickness = army size, temperature graph beneath). 2. Software Tools Tool type What it offers Spreadsheets (Excel, Google Sheets) Built-in charting tools for quick visual representation · pivot tables and custom formulas to analyse complex data and highlight key insights Creative design applications (Adobe Illustrator, Canva) Advanced design tools producing more sophisticated and visually appealing visualisations · add graphics, text and visual elements so output is both informative and engaging Combining applications (Excel + Tableau + Google Data Studio) Integrate data from different sources , apply forecasting models , display real-time insights through dashboards · lets businesses compare current data against predicted trends 2.1 Evolution of Hardware and Software Factor Impact on data analytics Processing power Enables efficient analysis of large and complex datasets · supports advanced analytics using complex algorithms · enabled machine learning · allows real-time analytics · contributed to the rise of cloud computing , making advanced tools accessible without expensive hardware Storage and memory Enables organisations to retain large datasets · supports more complex models and algorithms · enables machine learning , which relies on large training datasets · allows real-time analytics · enabled data warehousing — central storage supporting deeper analysis Communication media Internet and mobile devices allow data collection from a wide range of sources · faster, more reliable communication makes real-time collection and analytics possible · enabled cloud computing · supports collaboration and sharing of insight · enhances visualisation and data-driven decision-making The pattern in all three: each factor enabled bigger datasets → advanced analytics → machine learning → real-time → cloud . If you learn that chain you can answer any of the three. 3. Identifying Patterns The five steps: 1. COLLECT DATA from surveys, transactions or other sources 2. CLEAN AND ORGANISE remove duplicates, handle missing values, transform format 3. EXPLORE use visualisation, statistical analysis or ML to uncover insight 4. COMPARE DATASETS across time periods, groups or categories 5. PREDICTIVE ANALYTICS use ML to identify relationships and predict future trends 4. OLAP — Online Analytical Processing OLAP is a data analysis technique enabling business intelligence and decision-making. It is software allowing users to analyse and manipulate large, multi-dimensional datasets stored in a data warehouse. How it works: data is organised into a cube-like structure , where each dimension represents a different aspect — time, geography, product, customer. The cube makes complex analysis fast. The Four Techniques Technique What it does Example Used for Slicing Selects a single layer of the cube — filtering one dimension Only electronics sales in Australia Focusing on one category or condition Dicing Analyses a subset across multiple dimensions Electronics vs clothing, in Sydney and Melbourne, during Q1 Side-by-side comparisons Drill-down Breaks summary data into more detailed levels Country → state → city sales Finding specific contributors to a trend Roll-up Combines detailed data into a higher-level summary Total sales across all cities or countries Getting the big-picture overview Confusing pair — Slicing vs Dicing Slice = one dimension filtered, one flat layer of the cube. Dice = multiple dimensions filtered at once, a smaller sub-cube. One cut versus several. Confusing pair — Drill-down vs Roll-up Drill-down goes more detailed (summary → specifics). Roll-up goes less detailed (specifics → summary). Opposite directions on the same hierarchy. Worked scenarios: Scenario Technique Retail manager wants total sales per product category across all of Australia rather than individual cities Roll-up Marketing analyst wants only electronics sales in Q1 2024, ignoring other categories Slicing Manager knows electronics sell best overall and wants to know which specific city contributed most Drill-down Company wants to compare electronics and clothing in Sydney and Melbourne during Q1 Dicing 5. Enterprise Data Warehousing A data warehouse is a central storage system collecting and storing large amounts of data from different sources within an organisation. Unlike regular databases storing current, day-to-day data, a warehouse is designed to store historical data , allowing identification of trends and patterns over long periods. Key features: CENTRALISED combines data from multiple sources HISTORICAL stores data over long periods STRUCTURED, REFINED cleaned and organised for analysis SUPPORTS VISUALISATION used to create charts, dashboards and reports How EDWs Improve Visualisation Function Effect Analysis of historical trends and patterns Stores large volumes over long periods, allowing analysis of seasonal sales or customer behaviour . Historical data is compared with current data, visualising change over time. Supports predictive insights , anticipating future demand Correlation with current data Combines historical with real-time data, letting businesses compare past and present performance. Visualisation tools display these relationships, showing how current performance aligns with past patterns. Businesses adjust strategy when current trends diverge from history Data refinement / optimisation Supports cleaning and transforming data — removing errors, duplicates and inconsistencies. Refined data improves the quality and reliability of visualisations, revealing hidden patterns 6. Data Integrity Before creating any visualisation, assess data integrity to ensure the result is accurate and reliable. Factor What it means The question to ask Ownership Who controls and maintains the data — the collector, the owning organisation, or the visualisation team. Also determines who has authority to make corrections Are accountable people responsible for maintaining accuracy? Data with clear ownership is more trustworthy because someone is responsible for correcting errors Source The origin — data type, format and method of collection , including processing, cleaning methods and storage location Does it come from a reliable, appropriate source? Data collected automatically from trusted systems is generally more reliable than unknown or manually collected data Validation Verifying the accuracy and completeness of the data — checking anomalies, missing data, outliers and errors Is the dataset accurate and complete enough for meaningful visualisation? Poor validation leads to misleading graphs, incorrect trends and poor decisions Risk The likelihood of data corruption, errors or privacy concerns — breaches, loss, unauthorised access Could the data expose sensitive information, become corrupted or be manipulated? High-risk data may not be safe or ethical to visualise publicly Scope of visible information How much of the dataset the visualisation actually shows Is anything important being hidden by the framing? Types and depth of insight What kinds of conclusions the data can legitimately support Can this data actually answer the question being asked of it? 6.1 Bias Bias in data collection occurs when certain groups or variables are over- or underrepresented , producing skewed results that don't reflect reality. Source of bias What to evaluate Accuracy Are the underlying figures correct and complete? Audience Is the visualisation shaped to tell a particular audience what it wants to hear? Data source Does the source have an agenda, or systematically miss part of the population? Unconscious bias Assumptions the designer isn't aware they're making — in what to include, how to scale axes, which comparison to draw 7. Big Data — The Five Vs V Definition Handling Volume The massive amount of data generated from web apps, IoT devices and transaction records. Traditional storage struggles at scale Cloud-based storage so valuable information isn't lost to storage limits Velocity The speed at which data flows in — real-time social updates, high-frequency trading records. Provides opportunities for timely insight Stream processing frameworks and in-memory systems to capture and act in near real-time Variety The many different formats — traditional structured, unstructured (free text, images, video), and semi-structured (JSON, XML) with organisational properties but no strict schema NoSQL databases and data lakes with schema-on-read frameworks Veracity The accuracy and reliability of data. Great quantity from various sources means noise and errors leading to poor decisions Data cleaning, validation and verification tools Value The real-world benefit — optimising operations, identifying marketing opportunities Advanced analytics, machine learning and AI transforming raw information into actionable insight Data Science covers three Vs (volume, variety, velocity). Data Visualisation adds veracity and value . Know all five. 8. Interrogating a Data Visualisation Interrogating means closely examining and analysing the information in a visualisation to draw insight, identify trends and make decisions. The key questions: What is the PURPOSE of the visualisation? What TRENDS, PATTERNS or ANOMALIES are visible? Are there any OUTLIERS or unusual data points? What ASSUMPTIONS is the visualisation making? 8.1 Interpreting What You See Step What to check 1. Understand the chart type Line → trends over time · Bar → compare categories · Pie → proportions of a whole 2. Examine the axes What is being measured · units used · scale of the graph 3. Look for patterns Trends · increases or decreases · clusters · gaps or unusual results 4. Contextualise Does the graph show the full story ? Is more information needed? Are variables missing? 8.2 Aggregation Aggregation means combining many data values into one summary value — sum, average (mean), count, median. Benefits Limitations Simplifies large datasets · makes trends easier to identify · provides a high-level overview May hide important details · can mask outliers or unusual results 8.3 Filtering Filtering displays only specific parts of a dataset, helping users focus on relevant information. Benefits Limitations Simplifies large datasets · identifies trends and relationships · allows targeted analysis · makes dashboards interactive Important data may be hidden · can lead to biased conclusions if too much data is excluded Common uses: customer feedback by age group · sales by region or product · web traffic by device type. 8.4 The Effect of Outliers An outlier is a data point very different from the rest. Outliers can reveal Outliers can damage Errors in data entry · unusual but valid events · important insights Skew averages · distort trends · mislead viewers if ignored What analysts should do: decide whether it is an error or a meaningful result , and investigate before removing it . 8.5 Reasoning Reasoning means using logic and critical thinking to interpret data and draw conclusions. Good reasoning includes Why it matters Identifying trends — increases, decreases, seasonal patterns, relationships between variables Helps make informed decisions Assessing causality — what may have caused this? Could there be multiple causes? Prevents incorrect conclusions Avoiding bias — base conclusions on evidence, not assumption or opinion Supports evidence-based analysis Questioning assumptions — does the visualisation show the full story? Guards against being misled ⚠️ Correlation is not causation. Two variables moving together does not prove one caused the other. Naming a possible third cause is a Band 6 move. 9. Dashboards A dashboard is a single screen bringing together a small set of metrics with enough context to support a decision. It turns raw tables into ranked lists, small trends and clear status, so people know where to look first and what to do next . 9.1 The Narrative Approach Dashboards work better when they read like a short story: give the user a setup , a change , and a next step . People remember sequences. If the screen says what changed and why, they stop hunting through charts and start acting. 9.2 Visual Hierarchy People read what is heavy, close and high-contrast first. In left-to-right languages they scan in a Z : top-left → top-right → bottom-left → bottom-right. Put critical numbers on that path. TOP Status and targets — the "are we good?" line MIDDLE Trends and comparisons that explain the movement BOTTOM Details, owners and links that route follow-up work 9.3 Layout, Colour and Consistency Principle Rules Layout Use size and whitespace to signal priority , not as decoration. Keep a simple grid with even gutters — aligned cards read as orderly and trustworthy. Breaking the grid makes the page noisy and hides what matters Colour Use colour as a signal, not decoration . Assign stable meanings (neutrals for chrome, one highlight for "pay attention", a reserved colour for risk). Restrict the palette — 8 to 12 hues is plenty, avoid the rainbow. Back up colour with a second cue (icons, patterns, labels) so colour-blind users aren't blocked. Test contrast in dark and light themes Consistency Fix a grid, a spacing scale and a component set. Titles look the same everywhere, filters sit in the same place, legends behave the same. Don't surprise the user between tabs Cognitive load Remove non-data ink . Shorten labels. Round numbers to useful precision. Hide rare controls behind "More". Keep navigation shallow Limit choices Five precise filters beat fifteen vague ones. Ship with safe defaults so the first view is useful without clicks 9.4 Know Your Audience — The Six Questions 1. WHO is the intended audience? 2. WHY does this audience need to see this data? What decisions are they making? 3. WHAT key metrics provide the insight needed to support those decisions? 4. HOW will they use it — high-level monitoring, or drilling into detail? 5. WHEN will it be used — daily, weekly, or only in specific situations? 6. DESIGN how should it be structured to logically guide users through the data? 10. Evaluating Software Tools and UX 10.1 The Four Tool Categories Tool Strength Weakness Spreadsheets used to develop dashboards Accessible, familiar, low cost, quick to build Limited interactivity and scale; manual refresh Presentation software used to present analysis Strong for narrative and static reporting Not live; data becomes stale immediately Business analytics services, incl. 'as a service' products Scalable, live, professionally maintained, integrates sources Ongoing subscription cost; data leaves the organisation Custom software solutions Exactly fits the enterprise's needs High development cost, long build time, ongoing maintenance burden 10.2 Evaluating User Experience Analysis breaks something into components to understand how it works. Evaluation takes those findings and assesses their value, quality or effectiveness against criteria . Analysis is the breakdown . Evaluation is the judgement . Criterion Guiding question Evaluation method Clarity Is it easy to understand? Are labels and headings clear? Observation Usability Can users quickly find important information? Are filters and navigation easy? Task-based testing Accuracy Does it display information correctly, without misleading scales or missing data? Heuristic evaluation Accessibility Is text readable? Are colours distinguishable? Would colour-blind users understand it? User feedback Efficiency Can users gain insight quickly? Is there unnecessary clutter? Time on task Aesthetics Is it visually appealing and organised? Surveys and feedback Context and purpose Does it explain the purpose of the data clearly? Qualitative feedback 10.3 UX Factors in the Syllabus Factor Meaning Relevance to the audience The metrics shown must match the decisions that audience actually makes Audience interpretation How the audience will read it — including how they might misread it Customisation Whether users can tailor views, filters and layouts to their own needs Live analysis Whether data updates in real time or is a static snapshot 11. Developing a Visualisation The process: 1. RESEARCH AND SOURCE locate relevant, reliable datasets for the scenario 2. ORGANISE AND STORE structure the data appropriately, securely 3. GRAPHIC DEVELOPMENT apply design principles and digital tools 4. DESIGN AND DEVELOP represent trends, patterns and relationships and illustrate predictive analysis with big data 5. SECURE implement cybersecurity and data backup 11.1 Maintaining Data Security Method What it covers Cybersecurity Access control, encryption, authentication, firewalls, protecting against unauthorised access and breach Data backup Regular copies stored separately so data can be restored after loss, corruption or attack 12. Confusing Terms — Quick Reference Term Meaning Don't confuse with Slicing Filter one dimension Dicing — filter multiple dimensions Drill-down Summary → detail Roll-up — detail → summary Aggregation Combining values into one summary Filtering — showing only part of the data Analysis Breaking into components Evaluation — judging against criteria Data warehouse Historical data, central, for analysis Database — current, day-to-day operations Structured data Fixed schema Semi-structured — JSON, XML · Unstructured — text, images Outlier A point far from the rest An error — an outlier may be valid Correlation Two variables move together Causation — one causes the other Line chart Trends over time Bar chart — comparing categories · Pie chart — proportions Ownership Who is accountable for the data Source — where it came from Validation Checking accuracy and completeness Verification — confirming it matches the original Infographic Static, single point in time Dashboard — live, interactive, decision-oriented See also: Terminology | Data Science | Intelligent Systems | Enterprise Project | MOC

title: Enterprise Project
text: Enterprise Project — HSC Final Notes ✅ Named topic in the Trial (Task 4). The smallest unit, but it carries the implementation and testing content that appears in every scenario question. Outcomes: EC-12-08, EC-12-10, EC-12-11 Terminology: Terminology · Index: MOC 1. The Four Project Phases 1. IDENTIFYING AND DEFINING 2. RESEARCHING AND PLANNING 3. PRODUCING AND IMPLEMENTING 4. TESTING AND EVALUATING 2. Identifying and Defining 2.1 Tools and Processes for Managing and Documenting Development Tool / process Purpose Problem definition States clearly what the system must solve, before any solution is designed Time and resource management, incl. Gantt charts Schedules tasks, milestones and deadlines , showing which activities run concurrently An iterative approach Building in repeated cycles, refining with each pass rather than completing everything once Production process and technical skills The methods and capabilities required to actually build the system Testing and evaluation Verifying the system works and judging whether it met its purpose 2.2 The Changing Nature of Enterprise Change Effect on project development Offshore development Work contracted to teams overseas — lower cost, but time-zone, communication and quality-control challenges Working remotely Teams distributed rather than co-located — requires online collaboration tools and clear documentation Freelance work Specialist skills engaged per-project rather than employed — flexible and cost-effective, but less continuity Enabling the growth of start-ups Low-cost cloud infrastructure and remote talent let small enterprises build systems that once required large capital 3. Researching and Planning 3.1 Tools Supporting Design and Development Tool What it does Online collaboration Shared documents, version control and communication across a distributed team Time / task action plans Break the project into scheduled tasks with owners and deadlines Process diary, incl. ongoing evaluation Running record of decisions, problems and changes — evidence of the iterative process Budget Costs the resources, licences, hardware and labour required System flowcharts Show the logical steps the system performs Data flow diagrams Show how data moves between entities, processes and stores Decision trees Represent logical decision-making as branching conditions and outcomes Confusing pair — System flowchart vs Data flow diagram A flowchart shows the sequence of logic — what happens, in order, with decisions. A DFD shows where data goes — sources, processes, stores and destinations. Flowchart = how it thinks . DFD = where information travels . 3.2 Thinking Skills Skill Applied to Computational thinking Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms — see Intelligent Systems §7 Design thinking Understanding users and iterating solutions — see §4.3 below Systems thinking Seeing how components interact as a whole rather than in isolation 3.3 Collaborating and Managing Criteria Criterion Meaning Designing for ease of operation and maintenance Building so that non-experts can run it and future developers can modify it Clarifying each of the relevant informatics within the new system Identifying what information the system handles and how it transforms it Outlining the role of participants, data and components Who does what, what data flows where, which components are responsible Negotiating user/client needs and wants Distinguishing what the client needs from what they want , within budget and time Working collaboratively Shared responsibility, clear communication, agreed processes 4. Producing and Implementing 4.1 Tools to Inform Requirements and Limitations Tool Strength Interviews Deep, qualitative understanding of individual user needs Surveys Broad, quantitative data from many users quickly Analytical reports Existing documented evidence about the problem domain Prototypes A working model users can react to — surfaces requirements they couldn't articulate Presentations of research results Communicates findings to stakeholders and secures agreement 4.2 Development Approaches Approach How it works Best for Waterfall (structured) Linear and sequential — each phase completes before the next begins Well-defined, stable requirements; safety-critical work Agile Iterative and incremental — repeated short cycles with continuous client involvement Evolving requirements; fast-moving projects Prototyping Build a working model early, refine it based on feedback When requirements are unclear and users need something to react to End-user The users themselves develop the system, typically with spreadsheets or low-code tools Small, local solutions where users know the problem best Outsourcing Development contracted to an external provider When the skills don't exist in-house, or cost favours it Confusing pair — Waterfall vs Agile Waterfall fixes requirements at the start; working software appears only at the end ; changing late is very costly. Agile expects requirements to change; working software appears every iteration ; total cost and time are harder to predict. 4.3 Design Thinking 1. EMPATHISE understand the needs and challenges of end-users 2. DEFINE state the problem clearly 3. IDEATE generate possible solutions 4. PROTOTYPE build a testable model of the solution 5. TEST evaluate with real users and iterate A prototype's purpose is to test ideas and gather feedback before committing to full development, reducing the risk of building the wrong thing. 4.4 Risk Analysis Risk analysis identifies what could go wrong during a project so those risks can be prevented or mitigated before they occur, rather than reacted to afterwards. Risk type Examples Security risks Data breach, unauthorised access, malware Technical risks Hardware failure, integration incompatibility, data loss Financial risks Budget overrun, unexpected licensing costs Time / scheduling risks Missed deadlines, dependency delays, scope creep Human risks Staff turnover, insufficient training, user resistance Reducing security risk: encryption, access control and authentication, regular backups, staff training, security audits. 4.5 Hardware and Software Integration Why it matters: new components must work with the existing enterprise environment, or the system fails at deployment regardless of how well it was built. What to consider: Compatibility with existing hardware, operating systems and software Data migration — can existing data be transferred without loss? Interoperability — will the new system exchange data with current systems? Capacity — can existing infrastructure handle the additional load? Cost of any required upgrades 4.6 Training Why train before implementation: users who don't understand the system make errors, resist the change, and undermine the return on the investment. Training reduces errors, increases adoption and shortens the productivity dip after go-live. Methods: face-to-face workshops · online modules and tutorials · user manuals and documentation · mentoring by a super-user · help desk support. 4.7 System Implementation Methods Method How it works Risk Direct Old system switched off , new one switched on — a straight swap across the whole organisation at once Highest risk — no fallback. Cheapest and fastest Parallel Old and new systems run together for a period Lowest risk — the old system is a fallback. Most expensive , duplicated effort Pilot New system trialled with a small group first, then rolled out Low risk, limited disruption if it fails Phased Introduced one module or department at a time Moderate risk, slower, integration complexity during transition The recommendation questions they ask: Hospital management system → parallel . Patient safety means you cannot afford a gap; the cost of duplication is justified by the consequence of failure. Banking system → parallel over direct, for the same reason — financial records cannot be lost or corrupted, and a fallback is essential. 4.8 Testing Methodologies Methodology What it checks Functional testing That every function of the system performs correctly against its specification Live data The system using real operational data to validate behaviour Simulated data Artificially created data, including edge cases that rarely occur naturally Beta testing Real users evaluate the system before full release Volume testing Whether the system handles very large amounts of data without performance loss Acceptance testing The client confirms the system meets their requirements Why use multiple methodologies rather than one: each detects a different class of fault. Functional testing finds logic errors but not performance problems. Volume testing finds scaling problems but not usability problems. Beta testing finds usability problems but not edge cases. Relying on one leaves whole categories of defect undetected. 5. Testing and Evaluating 5.1 Verification vs Validation Question it answers Meaning Verification Are we building the system right ? Does it meet the specifications ? Is it free of defects? Validation Are we building the right system? Does it meet the user's actual needs and solve the real problem? A system can be perfectly verified — flawlessly built to spec — and completely fail validation , because the spec described the wrong thing. 5.2 The Five Evaluation Activities Activity Purpose Evaluating test data Confirms the system produces correct output across normal, boundary and invalid inputs before deployment Trialling operation and maintenance documentation Ensures the documentation actually works for the people who will run and maintain the system — supports long-term success after the developers leave Reviewing the impact of implementation Assessing effects across the organisation — see §5.3 Modifying designs to improve functionality Using user feedback to identify shortcomings and refine the system Testing, evaluating and maintaining Ongoing after deployment, not a one-off event 5.3 Reviewing Organisational Impact Aspect How it may be affected Employees New skills required, changed roles, resistance, possible displacement Processes and workflows Tasks performed differently, some eliminated, new steps introduced Customers and clients Service speed, accuracy and experience change Finances Implementation and training costs against efficiency gains Data and information New data collected, new storage and security obligations The environment Energy consumption, hardware disposal, reduced paper use 5.4 Test Data Categories Category Definition Example (age must be 0–120) Normal / valid Typical expected values 25 Boundary Values at the edges of the valid range 0, 120 Extreme / invalid Values outside the range, or the wrong type −5, 200, "abc" Why each matters: normal data proves the system works in ordinary use. Boundary data catches off-by-one errors, the most common logic fault. Invalid data proves the system rejects bad input gracefully rather than crashing. 5.5 Why Continuous Testing After Deployment Requirements change as the enterprise changes The operating environment changes — new hardware, operating systems, integrations New defects surface only under real-world load and unusual conditions Security threats evolve , so what was secure at launch may not remain so User feedback reveals usability problems invisible during development 6. Exam Question Bank Straight from the unit deck. These are the shapes the questions take. Design thinking Which stage focuses on understanding the needs and challenges of end-users? Which stage involves generating possible solutions? What is the purpose of creating a prototype? Thinking and design tools Which tool visualises how users interact with a system? Which project management tool schedules tasks, milestones and deadlines? Which thinking tool represents logical decision-making processes? Risk analysis What is the purpose of conducting a risk analysis? Identify four common types of risk. Name one strategy to reduce security risks. Integration and training Why is hardware and software integration important? What should be considered when integrating new software with existing systems? Why should end-users receive training before implementation? Suggest two training methods. Implementation methods Which method introduces the system to the entire organisation at once ? → Direct Which allows old and new to operate together ? → Parallel Which introduces it to a small group first? → Pilot Which introduces it one module or department at a time ? → Phased Testing methodologies Which checks every function performs correctly? → Functional Which uses real operational data ? → Live data Which uses artificially created data? → Simulated data Which allows real users to evaluate before release? → Beta Which determines whether the system handles very large data volumes ? → Volume Extension — higher order Which implementation method for a hospital management system ? Justify. Why is risk analysis important in an implementation plan? How does design thinking contribute to successful development? Why is user training essential? Compare parallel and direct implementation. Which for a banking system , and why? Why include multiple testing methodologies rather than one? Testing and evaluating What is the difference between verification and validation ? Why evaluate test data before deployment? Identify four types of test data and explain why each matters. How does trialling maintenance documentation support long-term success? What aspects of the organisation should be evaluated after implementation? How can user feedback modify design and improve functionality? Why do systems require continuous testing, evaluation and maintenance? 7. Confusing Terms — Quick Reference Term Meaning Don't confuse with Verification Built right — meets the spec Validation — the right system, meets user needs Direct implementation Whole organisation at once, no fallback Parallel — both run together Pilot Small group of users first Phased — one module or department at a time Waterfall Linear, sequential, fixed requirements Agile — iterative, expects change Prototyping Build a model to clarify requirements Agile — a whole development methodology Functional testing Every function against spec Acceptance testing — the client confirms Live data Real operational data Simulated data — artificially generated Boundary data At the edges of valid range Invalid data — outside the range System flowchart Sequence of logic DFD — movement of data Gantt chart Tasks, milestones, deadlines over time Decision tree — branching logic Needs What the client must have Wants — what they would like Offshore development Work sent overseas Outsourcing — contracted externally, may be local See also: Terminology | Data Science | Intelligent Systems | Data Visualisation | MOC

title: Intelligent Systems
text: Intelligent Systems — HSC Final Notes ✅ Named topic in the Trial (Task 4). 15 lessons across 5 weeks. Outcomes: EC-12-01, EC-12-02, EC-12-03, EC-12-04, EC-12-05, EC-12-06, EC-12-07, EC-12-08, EC-12-10, EC-12-11 Terminology: Terminology · Index: MOC 1. Decision Support Systems A decision support system (DSS) is an interactive computer-based system that helps individuals and organisations make decisions by analysing large sets of data. It combines data , sophisticated analytical models and user-friendly software to support decision-making, especially in complex and uncertain environments. 1.1 The Three Categories of Decision-Making Category Definition Human involvement Structured Routine, repetitive decisions with clear rules and known outcomes None or minimal — the system decides and acts Semi-structured Some elements can be automated, but judgement is still required The system recommends , a human decides Unstructured Novel, complex decisions with no clear procedure . Depend on experience, intuition and negotiation The system informs discussion , humans decide The tell in a scenario question: ask who makes the final call . Nobody → structured. System suggests, human confirms → semi-structured. Humans debating with data as one input → unstructured. 1.2 Worked Classification Scenario Type Why Supermarket automatically reorders stock below a threshold, no human involvement Structured Fixed rule, system acts alone Factory shift scheduling follows strict rules, updates weekly without manager input Structured Rule-driven, no judgement Airline route optimisation automatically updates routes before each flight Structured Calculation against known variables Loan approval auto-approves or rejects standard applications; staff review only borderline cases Structured Rules decide; exceptions escalate Financial advisor software suggests investments; the advisor makes the final decision Semi-structured System recommends, human decides Medical diagnosis assistant suggests diagnoses; the doctor confirms or adjusts Semi-structured System supports professional judgement Marketing dashboard shows feedback and trends; the manager uses experience and intuition Semi-structured Data informs, intuition decides City transport planning — models, pollution data and public surveys discussed in meetings Unstructured No procedure; negotiation and competing priorities University expansion — forecasts and financials plus community feedback and long-term goals Unstructured Novel, value-laden, no clear rule 1.3 Risks of Relying on a DSS Over-reliance — users stop applying their own judgement Garbage in, garbage out — poor data produces confidently wrong recommendations Bias embedded in the data or rules is applied consistently and invisibly Lack of transparency — users can't tell why a recommendation was made Accountability gap — who is responsible when an automated decision causes harm? 2. Expert Systems An expert system mimics the decision-making of a human expert in a specific domain using a knowledge base of facts and rules. 2.1 Applications Diagnosis medical, mechanical fault-finding Monitoring continuous observation against expected parameters Process control adjusting an industrial process in real time Scheduling allocating time, staff, machines Planning sequencing actions to reach a goal 2.2 The Three Key Features Component Contains Function Knowledge base Facts and rules Stores domain knowledge Inference engine The rule base — a set of IF–THEN rules Applies judgement and reasoning to the knowledge base and the user's responses to reach a decision User interface Input forms, output displays Allows the user to enter data and receive recommendations Some systems add an explanation module (explains how the decision was made) and a data store (keeps input and results for later analysis). 2.3 Two Kinds of Knowledge Source Nature Factual knowledge Textbooks and shared resources, agreed upon by experts Objective, verifiable Heuristic knowledge Experience and reasoning — "rules of thumb" Judgement-based, harder to codify 2.4 Rules and Boolean Operators Rules take the form IF … THEN , combined with Boolean operators: AND && both conditions must be true OR || either condition may be true IF (feathers && beak || 2 legs) THEN it is a bird 2.5 Forward vs Backward Chaining Forward chaining Backward chaining Also called Data-driven reasoning Goal-driven reasoning Starts with Known facts / conditions A goal or hypothesis Process Applies rules to derive new conclusions until it reaches a goal Works backward to check whether the facts support the goal Best when You have data and want to know what it means You have a suspected answer and want to confirm it Worked example — medical diagnosis Knowledge base: Rule 1: IF fever AND cough THEN might have the flu Rule 2: IF sore throat THEN might have a cold Rule 3: IF body aches THEN might have the flu Rule 4: IF might have the flu THEN recommend rest and fluids Forward chaining — known facts: fever, cough, body aches. Check which rules have matching conditions Rule 1 (fever AND cough) is true → conclude: might have the flu Rule 3 (body aches) also true → confirms the conclusion That conclusion triggers Rule 4 → recommend rest and fluids Backward chaining — goal: does the patient have the flu? Find a rule that concludes "might have the flu" → Rule 1 or Rule 3 Ask: does the patient have a fever? → yes Ask: does the patient have a cough? → yes Both true, so Rule 1 is satisfied → the goal is confirmed Which is better? Forward chaining suits many inputs, unknown outcome (monitoring, sensors). Backward chaining suits few candidate outcomes, expensive data collection — it only asks the questions it needs. 3. Evolution of Expert Systems 3.1 Factors That Advanced Rule-Based Systems into Probabilistic Ones Factor Effect Processing power Enables analysis of vast datasets instantly Data availability and access Digital records improve accuracy and coverage Hardware costs Falling costs make powerful infrastructure affordable to deploy Neural networks Allow interpretation with nuance and handling of uncertainty Webometrics Measurement and analysis of web data ensures real-time updates refine decision-making 3.2 Changing Needs Driving Proliferation Driver Meaning IoT — Internet of Things Networked physical devices collecting continuous data IoMe — Internet of Me Personalised, individual-centred connected services and data Industry 4.0 The integration of automation, data exchange and intelligent systems into manufacturing and enterprise 3.3 The Progression Stage What happens Rule-based expert system Fixed IF–THEN rules, static knowledge base, no learning Probabilistic expert system Adds probabilities to handle uncertainty (Bayesian networks) Learning expert system Uses historical data to improve decisions (machine learning) Fully intelligent system Integrates multiple inputs, adapts, predicts and may act autonomously Example: MYCIN (1970s) diagnosed disease using fixed rules. Modern medical AI learns from millions of patient records, predicts likelihoods and updates its knowledge automatically. 3.4 Expert Systems vs Intelligent Systems Expert system (rule-based) Intelligent system Definition Mimics human experts using facts and IF–THEN rules Learns, adapts and reasons under uncertainty Reasoning Deterministic — fixed rules only Probabilistic — handles incomplete data Learning Limited — rules must be manually updated Machine learning improves decisions over time Inputs Requires high-quality structured knowledge Integrates text, voice, images, IoT data Example MYCIN Google Assistant, self-driving cars, recommendation engines 4. Intelligent Agents 4.1 Simplistic vs Complex Feature Simplistic agent Complex agent Definition Follows predefined rules or simple logic. Does not learn or adapt Uses machine learning, reasoning and adaptation to improve over time and predict outcomes Behaviour Reactive — responds directly to specific conditions Proactive or adaptive — anticipates and adjusts Knowledge base Small, fixed IF–THEN rule set Large and dynamic , updated through data and experience Probability / learning None — purely deterministic Probabilistic reasoning, deep learning, reinforcement learning Processing needs Low High — greater power and data access Domain Simplistic Complex Healthcare Rule-based diagnosis checklist IBM Watson Health using probability Transport Traffic light timer Smart traffic system adapting to live flow Home automation Fixed schedule thermostat Nest thermostat learning user habits Finance Fixed budget calculator Predictive trading system Customer service Scripted chatbot Conversational AI using NLP and intent recognition 4.2 Search Engine Agents Predictive search strings — predictive text guesses the next word using natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning . You type "This weekend, I'm planning to" → it suggests "go", "visit", "relax". Voice assistants — capture speech, convert it to text, interpret intent using NLP, then query and respond. More complex than text agents because they must handle accent, background noise and continuous speech . 5. Inference Engine Techniques Inference engines are the core component of an expert system, responsible for drawing conclusions from data and rules. Technique What it does Truth maintenance system (TMS) Tracks which beliefs or facts are true in a dynamic environment . When new information is added or existing information revised, it consistently updates all related facts Hypothetical reasoning Explores "what-if" scenarios — tests different hypotheses or assumptions to determine possible outcomes Heuristic knowledge Uses practical "rules of thumb" based on experience rather than formal proof Fuzzy logic Reasoning that is approximate rather than precise — handles uncertainty and imprecision. Values between true and false, not just 0 or 1 Ontology classification Organises knowledge into categories or concepts and defines the relationships between them , so the system can reason about data in a structured way Confusing pair — Heuristic knowledge vs Fuzzy logic Heuristic = the rule is a shortcut from experience ("if it's cloudy in the morning, expect rain"). Fuzzy logic = the value itself is imprecise ("the room is somewhat warm" = 0.7 warm). Heuristic is about where the rule came from. Fuzzy is about how precisely it's expressed. 6. Hardware for Intelligent Systems Hardware What it is Features Processing challenges Examples Biometrics Measures human physical or behavioural characteristics for identification and authentication Unique to each individual · requires sensors or scanners · high accuracy but needs calibration and secure storage Encrypting sensitive personal data · matching accuracy in poor lighting or noise · ethical and privacy concerns Fingerprint smart locks · Face ID · biometric attendance Haptics Uses touch, vibration or motion feedback to simulate physical interaction Tactile feedback via motors or actuators · both input (touch detection) and output (vibration/force) · enhances realism Real-time response with minimal delay · high bandwidth · hard to synchronise with visual and audio VR gloves in surgery simulators · force-feedback steering Touch and gesture Sensors detecting physical contact or body movement Intuitive natural interface · multi-touch and gesture recognition · sensitive to environment Gesture recognition algorithms · misreads from movement noise · high processing for real-time recognition Industrial touchscreens · gesture-controlled kiosks VR / AR Cameras, sensors and controllers track motion and overlay virtual content Immersive 3D interaction · motion and spatial tracking · high graphic demand Synchronising visuals and motion · high CPU/GPU load · latency affects experience AR-assisted surgery · VR maintenance trainers Voice and sound Captures spoken commands or environmental sound via microphones Converts sound waves to digital data · requires NLP · keyword or continuous recognition Background noise · complex language understanding · accent and pronunciation variation Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant · call-centre systems Microcontrollers Compact ICs performing specific control tasks in an embedded system Contains CPU, memory and I/O ports · real-time processing · cost-effective and energy efficient Limited memory and speed · requires efficient code · difficulty integrating multiple complex inputs Arduino in IoT devices · smart appliances Sensors Detect and measure physical conditions and convert them to digital signals Converts real-world data into measurable values · analogue or digital · crucial for system awareness Calibration and accuracy · large volumes needing real-time processing · sensor drift or failure Temperature sensors · proximity sensors in robotics Actuators and motors Convert electrical signals into physical motion Includes servo, stepper and DC motors · provides feedback via sensors Precise timing and calibration · energy and thermal management · synchronising with sensor feedback loops Robotic arms · smart windows · vehicle components The system loop to memorise: Sensors collect → microcontroller processes against the knowledge base via the inference engine → actuators execute the decision. Sensors are input . Actuators are output . Microcontrollers are the control centre . 6.1 Worked Scenario Mapping System Input Inference engine processes Knowledge base holds Output Smart greenhouse Sensors (temperature, humidity, soil moisture) Rules for irrigation scheduling Historical crop condition data Automatic activation of irrigation motors Building security Biometric + motion sensors Matching captured images against the employee database Employee facial data and authorisation levels Security alert and door lock activation Voice warehouse assistant Microphone Speech-to-text interpretation and command logic Product codes and warehouse map data Verbal confirmation and on-screen updates VR safety training VR headset and haptic gloves Detection of unsafe gestures Safety rules and correct movement data Haptic feedback vibration alert Factory production robot Sensors Sensor data for position correction Assembly design patterns and alignment parameters Actuator movements for precision adjustment Fleet maintenance Engine sensors Rules identifying abnormal engine data Normal engine operation parameters Maintenance alert to fleet manager AR retail mirror Camera and motion sensors Body tracking and clothing overlay logic Clothing size data and 3D models AR visual simulation on screen 7. Computational Thinking in System Design Strategy Definition Example Why it matters Decomposition Breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts Designing an autonomous car by separating object detection, route planning and speed control Smaller tasks are easier to analyse and solve, leading to more efficient development Pattern recognition Identifying recurring patterns or trends in data or processes Facial recognition identifying the distance between eyes or nose shape Helps the system learn and predict more effectively Abstraction Focusing on important details while ignoring irrelevant information A navigation app focuses on roads, traffic and directions, ignoring building colours Reduces unnecessary complexity Algorithms Step-by-step instructions for solving a problem A store recommendation system suggesting products from user preferences Powers the decision-making process Worked — an energy efficiency advisor expert system Decomposition into subsystems: Subsystem Description User interface Collects user input and displays recommendations Knowledge base Stores expert knowledge as rules and facts Inference engine Applies logical reasoning to the knowledge base and user data Explanation module Explains how the decision was made Database / data store Keeps input and results for later analysis Pattern recognition — recurring input patterns become rules: Input
