pattern Recommendation High daily energy use + poor insulation Improve insulation High device count + long operation hours Switch to energy-efficient devices Low natural light + high lighting energy Install skylights or LED lighting Old appliances + frequent maintenance Upgrade appliances Abstraction — keep what matters: KEEP: building type · energy consumption (kWh/day) · insulation quality device types and usage hours · lighting type IGNORE: wall colour · window size · furniture layout · device brand names Algorithm: START INPUT building_type, insulation, device_count, energy_use IF insulation = "poor" AND energy_use > 50 THEN recommendation = "Improve insulation" ELSE IF device_count > 20 AND energy_use > 60 THEN recommendation = "Replace old devices with efficient ones" ELSE IF lighting_type != "LED" AND energy_use > 40 THEN recommendation = "Install LED lighting" ELSE recommendation = "Energy usage is optimal" OUTPUT recommendation END Modular design matters because new rules can be added later without rebuilding the system. 8. Communicating System Processes Tool Shows Read Flowchart Step-by-step logic in a process — the algorithm Top to bottom, left to right Data flow diagram (DFD) How data moves through the system Follow the arrows Infographic Simplifies complex processes for easy understanding . A static, single-point-in-time dashboard counts as an infographic Visually, at a glance 8.1 DFD Components Component What it is Named with External entities Sources or sinks of data — users, sensors Nouns (they are things) Processes Calculations, logic — they change the data Verbs (they are actions) Data stores Databases and files Nouns Data flows Arrows showing data movement Labelled with the data 8.2 DFD Levels Level Purpose Audience Level 0 (context diagram) The whole system as ONE process , with its inputs, outputs and external entities Big picture for managers and clients Level 1 Breaks the main process into sub-processes Helps programmers design modules and interfaces Worked — SmartLoan Expert System LEVEL 0 Process: Loan Decision System External entities: Bank Officer · Credit Bureau Data stores: Applicant Database · Loan Rules Database LEVEL 1 1.1 Collect Applicant Data 1.2 Retrieve Credit Report 1.3 Apply Lending Rules 1.4 Generate Decision Report Data stores: Applicant Database · Loan Rules Database · Decision Report Archive Flowchart for the same system: Start → Input applicant data → Check credit score IF < 600 → Reject → Check income-to-loan ratio IF > 40% → Review manually → Else → Approve → Display decision and reasoning End DFD vs flowchart — the distinction they examine: a DFD shows data movement ; a flowchart shows decision logic . They complement each other, they don't substitute. 9. Disruptive Effects Effect Explanation Multitasking vs digital distraction Productivity apps and AI assistants aim to help users multitask, but frequent interruptions decrease attention span and lower work quality Working differently to complete the same task Tasks become faster and more accurate but require new skills — giving clear voice commands, interpreting AI-generated results. Planning a trip traditionally means researching flights, hotels and activities separately; a travel AI automates it into a tailored itinerary Automation of processes Repetitive tasks performed by systems, reducing human effort and error. Improves efficiency and lowers cost but displaces workers . Automated warehouses use AI robots to pick, pack and ship faster than humans Impact of AI on employment Creates new jobs while eliminating others. Self-driving technology reduces demand for truck drivers but increases demand for AI engineers and vehicle technicians. Roles requiring creativity, emotional intelligence and complex decision-making are least likely to be replaced. Workers must reskill 9.1 Social vs Ethical Issues Definition Concerned with Social issues Challenges impacting individuals, communities or society when intelligent systems are developed and used Fairness, access , human rights, societal wellbeing Ethical issues Concerns about what is morally right or wrong in designing and using systems Values — fairness, transparency, accountability, responsible use Issue Category Job displacement due to AI automation Social Digital divide — unequal access to AI and technology Social AI in healthcare — access to AI-driven medical care Social Bias in AI algorithms Ethical Privacy violations — data misuse and surveillance Ethical Transparency of AI decisions Ethical AI in law enforcement, e.g. facial recognition Ethical AI weaponisation — military applications Ethical The distinguishing question: does it concern who is affected and how (social), or whether it is right (ethical)? Job losses are social. The bias causing them is ethical. 10. Intelligent Networks and IoT An intelligent network integrates devices and technologies to enhance operational efficiency, data management and decision-making. With IoT , it connects sensors, machines and servers for seamless communication and automation. 10.1 Infrastructure Requirements Component Role Networks with servers Central processing and coordination of device traffic Local storage On-device or on-premises — fast, no internet dependency Cloud storage Scalable, accessible anywhere, supports large IoT data streams End-point devices The sensors, actuators and user devices at the network edge Communication links Wired and wireless connections carrying data between endpoints, servers and cloud 10.2 Data in IoT Systems Where data comes from: sensors, users, APIs, devices, social media, enterprise databases. Who provides it: machines (IoT devices) · humans (forms, voice commands) · external systems (cloud services, APIs). How it's collected: real-time (continuous streams) · batch (daily uploads) · manual entry. How much to collect: enough for accurate decisions, but surplus data slows processing and wastes storage . Type Example Use Quantitative Temperature, heart rate, light intensity Measurable patterns Qualitative Voice input, text feedback User experience insights Structured Tables, spreadsheets, databases Easy to query Unstructured Images, videos, text logs Requires more processing 10.3 Data Processing Stages Stage What it does Example Cleaning Remove duplicates, fix missing values, correct errors Remove duplicate temperature readings caused by a sensor glitch Validation Check data meets specific rules and standards Ensure temperature readings fall within −20 °C to 60 °C Filtering Select relevant data, discard surplus Keep the average daily temperature instead of every second's reading Smart traffic system: IoT cameras collect thousands of images per hour. The system cleans (removes corrupted images), validates (checks timestamp and location tags) and filters (keeps only rush-hour data) before analysis. 10.4 Transmission Flow type Description Example Device-to-Device (D2D) Data exchanged directly between IoT devices Smart lights adjusting brightness from sensor input Device-to-Cloud Sensors send data to the cloud for storage or analysis Fitness tracker sending heart-rate data Cloud-to-Device Commands sent from cloud down to a device Cloud sends an alert to a phone app Impact on network performance: Structured data (small packets) transmits FASTER Unstructured data (images, video) uses MORE BANDWIDTH Surplus data (redundant readings) causes LAG and HIGHER COST Smart city network: filters air quality data locally at each sensor node , transmitting only hourly averages to the cloud — reducing network load while keeping insights fast and relevant. 11. Simulation, Data Modelling and Surveillance 11.1 Applications in Enterprise Application Use Education and training Simulated environments let learners practise safely and repeatedly Business analytics Modelling scenarios to forecast outcomes and support planning High-risk applications Testing decisions where real-world failure is dangerous or expensive — aviation, mining, medicine 11.2 Intelligent Systems in Surveillance Method Role CCTV Automated monitoring, motion detection, facial recognition Biometrics Identity verification and access control Customer loyalty Tracking purchase behaviour to profile and target customers Fraud prevention Detecting anomalous transactions against normal patterns Sniffing Intercepting and analysing network traffic Trolling Detecting and moderating hostile or manipulative online behaviour 12. Building Expert Systems 12.1 Rules, Facts and Decision Trees A decision tree is a data model that helps a system make choices by breaking decisions into simple IF–THEN steps. Each branch is a question or condition ( Is temperature > 30 °C? ). Each leaf is an outcome or action ( Turn on the cooling system ). Certainty factors attach a confidence value to a rule or conclusion, letting the system express how sure it is rather than a flat yes/no. Where things live: the knowledge base holds facts . The inference engine holds and applies the rules . Both are examinable and frequently confused. 12.2 Verifying Data Sources Verifying data sources is critical to ensuring a DSS provides reliable insight. Unverified data leads to harmful outcomes — a healthcare DSS acting on incorrect medication history risks dangerous drug interactions; a retail DSS on unverified sales forecasts causes excess inventory and holding costs. Check Questions to ask Source credibility Who collected it — government, university, private company? Is the source reputable? Is it biased (sponsored research, political influence)? Accuracy and timeliness When was it collected? Is it still relevant? Any updates or revisions? Compare with other sources Do other reputable sources report similar data? Where they differ, why? Collection methods Surveys, sensors or user input? Scientifically sound and free from bias? Large and representative sample? Transparency and documentation Is there a clear explanation of how data was collected? Are raw data and methodologies publicly available? Bias or manipulation Could the data have been altered or misrepresented? Is there an agenda behind its collection or reporting? 13. Evaluating Intelligent Systems 13.1 How Expert Systems Contribute to Efficiency Technology Contribution Supercomputers Process huge datasets very quickly. Combined with expert systems, enable real-time analysis and adjustment — critical in financial markets and emergency response. The IBM Summit supercomputer uses AI-driven expert systems to optimise energy usage and support medical research Digital assistants Provide hands-free, natural-language access to information and control Autonomous vehicles Integrate sensor, map and traffic data to make continuous driving decisions Streaming services Recommendation engines matching content to inferred preference The efficiency arguments: Analyse complex data in fields like climate science and genetics faster than traditional methods Store specialised knowledge accessibly, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated in real time Automate complex decision-making that would otherwise require substantial human expertise, reducing human involvement in supply chain management and predictive maintenance Adjust recommendations continuously as new data arrives 13.2 Assessing DSS Output Graph and compare proposed vs actual outputs. The gap between what the system predicted and what actually happened is the measure of its effectiveness. 14. Confusing Terms — Quick Reference Term Meaning Don't confuse with Structured decision Clear rules, system decides alone Semi-structured — system recommends, human decides Unstructured decision No procedure, judgement and negotiation Semi-structured — partly automatable Knowledge base Stores facts Inference engine — applies the rules Forward chaining Data-driven, starts with facts Backward chaining — goal-driven, starts with a hypothesis Factual knowledge Agreed, from textbooks Heuristic knowledge — from experience Heuristic knowledge Rule of thumb from experience Fuzzy logic — imprecise values Simplistic agent Fixed rules, reactive, no learning Complex agent — adaptive, probabilistic Expert system Deterministic, fixed rules Intelligent system — learns and adapts Sensors Input — detect and measure Actuators — output, create motion Microcontroller The control centre Sensors and actuators — the periphery Flowchart Shows decision logic DFD — shows data movement Level 0 DFD Whole system as one process Level 1 — broken into sub-processes Social issue Who is affected and how Ethical issue — whether it is right Relevant data Needed for the decision Surplus data — wastes storage, causes lag IoT Internet of Things — networked devices IoMe — Internet of Me, personalised services Decomposition Break into parts Abstraction — remove irrelevant detail See also: Terminology | Data Science | Data Visualisation | Enterprise Project | MOC

title: Principles of Cybersecurity
text: Principles of Cybersecurity — Final Notes ⚠️ NOT a named topic in the Trial (Task 4). The notification lists Intelligent Systems, Data Science, Data Visualisation and Enterprise Project . However: "The Year 11 course is assumed knowledge for the Year 12 course." Security concepts surface inside Data Science (privacy and legal issues), Data Visualisation (data integrity and security) and Enterprise Project (risk analysis). Revision priority: LOW. Read §1, §4 and §5 only unless you have time to spare. Terminology: Terminology · Index: MOC 1. The Core Vocabulary These four terms are constantly confused and are the foundation of everything else. Term Definition Threat An individual or group responsible for carrying out cyberattacks — or the potential source of harm Vulnerability A weakness in a system or process that can be taken advantage of by an attacker Risk The potential for harm when a threat exploits a vulnerability Exploit The act of illegally accessing systems, networks or data The relationship: a threat exploits a vulnerability , creating risk . No vulnerability, no risk — even with a threat present. 2. Social Networking Vulnerabilities Vulnerability Definition Impact on the individual Impact on the enterprise Mitigation Account access Unauthorised login using stolen or weak credentials Identity theft, leaked personal photos, financial fraud Employee accounts compromised, corporate data exposed, network breach risk Strong unique passwords · two-factor authentication (2FA) · avoid password reuse Account behaviour Risky or careless posting or sharing that exposes sensitive information Privacy loss, stalking, targeted phishing Leaked internal information, legal action, reputational damage Educate on safe sharing · use privacy settings · implement a clear social media policy Hosting platform security The protection the platform itself provides — or fails to provide Personal information stolen, increased spam and scam attempts Brand accounts hacked, customer data compromised, loss of trust Choose reputable platforms · monitor breach notifications · limit data shared with platforms Identity theft Stealing someone's personal information to impersonate them Financial loss, damaged credit, legal complications Fraudulent transactions in the business's name, supply chain compromise Limit publicly available personal data · monitor accounts · verify identity requests Phishing Deceptive messages or links tricking users into giving up private information Credentials stolen, malware installed Network access gained, ransomware deployed, funds misdirected Staff training · email filtering · verify senders · never click unverified links Evil twins Fake or impersonated accounts made to look like real people or brands Deceived into sharing information or money Brand impersonation, customer deception, reputational harm Account verification · report impersonation · monitor for fake brand accounts Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS . Named explicitly in the syllabus. 3. Cybercrime Threats to an Enterprise Threat How it operates Hacking Unauthorised access to systems, networks or data, exploiting technical vulnerabilities Phishing, including smishing Deceptive email or SMS tricking users into revealing credentials or installing malware Scamming Deception to obtain money or information directly from victims Bots and botnets Automated programs; a botnet is a network of compromised machines controlled remotely, used for DDoS attacks or spam Employee action causing a vulnerability Insider threat — careless or malicious behaviour opening a weakness. Often the largest single risk because it bypasses perimeter defences Common enterprise vulnerabilities: weak passwords · phishing susceptibility · unpatched software · insider threats · misconfigured cloud storage . 4. The Four Breach Attributes A cybersecurity breach occurs when unauthorised access is gained to data, systems or networks, resulting in loss, damage or exposure of information. Attribute Definition Examples of compromise Consequences Confidentiality Protecting sensitive data from unauthorised access, exposure or theft Personal records · financial data · trade secrets and IP Identity theft, fraud, corporate espionage · legal penalties · reputational damage Integrity Maintaining the accuracy, consistency and reliability of data Malware altering system data · unauthorised database edits · manipulation of financial or health records Incorrect business or government decisions · loss of trust in data systems · sector-wide disruption Availability Ensuring authorised users can access information and services when needed DDoS attacks · ransomware encryption · system crashes causing downtime Business interruption and lost revenue · inconvenience · disruption of critical services Privacy Protecting individuals' personal data from unauthorised exposure Leaked medical records · exposed financial records · disclosed personal identifiers Identity theft, scams, fraud · legal penalties under the Privacy Act 1988 · erosion of customer trust 4.1 Worked Classification These scenarios come straight from the deck. Note that most breaches compromise more than one attribute. Scenario Attributes compromised Email leak — employee sends a customer list to the wrong client Confidentiality · Privacy Altered financial records — insider changes transaction records Integrity Smart home device listening — voice recordings accessed by employees Confidentiality · Privacy Ransomware on hospital systems — patient data locked, doctors cannot access records Availability · (Confidentiality if exfiltrated) Fitness app data sold to advertisers without consent Privacy · Confidentiality DDoS attack on a bank — website unavailable for hours Availability Website defacement — homepage changed to display false messages Integrity Password database exposure — hashed passwords stolen Confidentiality · Privacy The tell for each: Confidentiality = someone saw it. Integrity = someone changed it. Availability = nobody can reach it. Privacy = it was personal data. 5. Legislation and Frameworks Framework Coverage Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) Sets out how organisations must handle personal information. Applies to organisations with annual turnover over $3 million and some small business operators Australian Privacy Principles (APPs) 13 principles governing collection, use, disclosure, governance, accountability, integrity, correction, and individuals' right of access. Technology neutral , so they adapt to changing technology. A breach is an "interference with the privacy of an individual" and can lead to regulatory action and penalties Consumer Data Right (CDR) In designated sectors such as banking and energy , mandates specific data handling with consumer consent and accreditation of data recipients GDPR (EU) The EU framework, built on 7 fundamental principles shaping collection, storage and processing of personal data Authorities: the OAIC (Office of the Australian Information Commissioner) enforces the Privacy Act. The ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre), part of ASD , provides business guidance. 6. Individual Privacy Protection Strategy What it does Password management Strong, unique passwords per service; a password manager with encryption Multi-factor authentication (MFA / 2FA) Requires a second factor, so a stolen password alone is insufficient Encryption Renders data unreadable without the key, protecting it in transit and at rest Secure networks Avoid unsecured public Wi-Fi; use a VPN when a public connection is unavoidable Personal behaviour Limiting what is shared publicly, checking privacy settings, verifying requests before responding Private vs personal information — personal information identifies you (name, date of birth, address, email, phone). Private information is what you choose not to disclose. The books you read are private but not personal; your date of birth is personal and should be kept private. 7. Confusing Terms — Quick Reference Term Meaning Don't confuse with Threat The actor or source of harm Vulnerability — the weakness they exploit Vulnerability A weakness in a system Risk — the potential harm arising from it Exploit The act of attacking Vulnerability — the opening that allows it Confidentiality Data not seen by the unauthorised Privacy — protection of personal data specifically Integrity Data not altered Availability — data reachable when needed Phishing Deception by email Smishing — by SMS Evil twin A fake account impersonating a real person or brand Identity theft — using a real person's details Bot A single automated program Botnet — a network of compromised machines Personal information Identifies you Private information — what you choose not to share DDoS Floods a service to deny availability Ransomware — encrypts data to deny availability and extort See also: Terminology | Data Science | Data Visualisation | Enterprise Project | MOC

selective sampling, underrepresentation of groups or measurement error Data cleaning Removing duplicates, fixing missing values and correcting errors Data dictionary Documentation of a database's text, CSV or JSON — without relationships or indexing Flowchart A diagram representing logic and decision-making , read top to bottom and left to right Foreign key A field referring to a primary key Technology using touch, vibration or motion feedback to simulate physical interaction HAVING An SQL clause filtering groups after GROUP BY , as distinct from filtering rows Heuristic knowledge input to reach a conclusion Infographic A visual simplifying complex processes for easy understanding; a static, single-point-in-time dashboard qualifies Informatics The study of the processing and by whom it was collected Microcontroller A compact integrated circuit containing CPU, memory and I/O ports, performing specific control tasks in an embedded system Multi-factor authentication (MFA) authority enforcing the Privacy Act OLAP Online analytical processing — software analysing large, multi-dimensional datasets organised in a cube structure Ontology classification Organising knowledge into categories and concepts and defining the relationships between them Ordinal A level of measurement using categories with a meaningful order but unequal gaps — satisfaction ratings, year level accuracy P Term Definition Parallel implementation Old and new systems run together for a period. information is collected, used, stored and disclosed Processed data Data cleaned, transformed or manipulated to make it easier to analyse Prototyping Building a working model early and refining it
